title: Meeting New People at a Language Exchange Café
summary: At a café language exchange, you trade languages with new people, write your languages on a sticker, say your name with a handshake, and ask follow-up questions.

sources.label: Taalcafé Language Exchange, Dutch Language Café

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Today we visit a language exchange in a café. We learn how the evening works, how to order and how to introduce yourself. Then we practise keeping a conversation going with new people.

items.prompt: Do you like meeting new people? Why or why not?
What do you usually say first when you meet someone new?
Which language would you like to practise with a native speaker?

blocks.title: Part 1: How a Language Exchange Works
paragraphs: A language exchange is a trade: you give something, and you get something. You help someone with your language, and they help you with theirs. For example, you speak Japanese and want to practise English. Then you look for an English speaker who wants to practise Japanese. Many language cafés split the time in half. You talk in one language for half an hour. Then you talk in the other language for half an hour. This way, both people get the same time to learn.

In this lesson, you visit the Dutch Language Café in The Hague. The Hague is a city in the Netherlands. On Thursday evenings, its language exchange starts at 19:30. When you arrive, you tell the host: I'm here for the language exchange.

But how do you find the right person in a busy room? The café gives you a language sticker. You write your languages on it and wear it. You write your native language and the languages you want to practise. Your native language is the first language you learned as a child. Other people look at your sticker and know your languages at once. They often ask too: Which languages do you speak? You answer: My native language is Japanese.

At 20:00, the speed exchange starts. You talk with one person for 3 minutes. Then you move to the next person. Why so short? This way, you meet many people quickly. Later, everyone sits at language tables, for example an English table.

Hi! Which languages do you speak?

blocks.title: Part 2: Ordering at the Café
paragraphs: At the Dutch Language Café, the Thursday ticket costs €11. The ticket pays for snacks and games. The snacks are things like popcorn and nuts. You ask the host: Are the snacks included? The host says yes. But drinks are not in the ticket, so you buy them at the bar.

On the menu, you see a funny name: koffie verkeerd. In English, koffie verkeerd is wrong coffee. Why wrong? A normal Dutch coffee has only a little milk. Koffie verkeerd has more milk than coffee, so it is the wrong way around. At the bar, you order: Can I have a koffie verkeerd, please? Then you ask: How much is it? It costs €4.00.
If you are hungry, you ask the waiter: What is an empanada? It is a small pastry, with cheese, meat or vegetables inside. An empanada costs €6.50.

Thank you. How much is it?

blocks.title: Part 3: Introducing Yourself
paragraphs: In the Netherlands, people shake hands when they meet someone new. At the same time, they say their name: Hi! I'm Sanne. Often they say only their first name. In Japan, many people bow, or bend forward, and say their family name. But for Dutch people, a hello without a name is rude, or not polite. Why? Dutch people like to be clear, so they start with a name. When you hear a new name, you say your name too. Then you say: Nice to meet you.

The first time you meet a Dutch person, do not ask: How are you? Many Dutch people use this question only with people they already know. A stranger is a person you do not know. If a stranger asks this, a Dutch person may think you met before. They may think they forgot you!

In a 3-minute speed exchange, you do not have much time. So say three things: your name, your city and why you study the language. Lucía from Spain says: Hi! I'm Lucía. I'm from Valencia. I study Dutch because I work in The Hague. The last part is the most useful. It gives people a question to ask, for example: Where do you work? Then Lucía asks: What about you?

images.alt: Two adults sitting at a small wooden café table in the evening, smiling and shaking hands across the table, each with a small blank sticker on their shirt, coffee cups on the table, warm lamps inside and a dark window behind.

items.prompt: Why should you not ask a Dutch stranger: How are you?
items.answer: They may think you met before.

rows.example: Hi, Sanne! Nice to meet you.

rows.meaning: to ask the same question back
rows.example: I'm from Osaka. What about you?

blocks.title: Part 4: Keeping the Conversation Going
paragraphs: The best tool for a long conversation is the follow-up question. This is a question about what the other person just said. Lucía says: I work at a hotel. A new question jumps to a new idea: Do you like football? A follow-up question stays with her idea: What do you do at the hotel?

Lucía also says: I moved here from Valencia. Each follow-up question uses one part of what she says. You ask about her reason: Really? Why did you move here? You ask about her city: What is Valencia like? You ask about time: How long have you lived here?

In 2017, scientists at Harvard University studied how strangers talk. People who asked more questions were liked more by their partners. Follow-up questions worked best of all. Why? A follow-up question shows that you are really listening.

At 21:30, the exchange ends. When you want to leave, end the conversation in a kind way. Do not just walk away. The other person gave you their time. So say thank you with kind words: It was nice to talk to you.

blocks.title: Scene: Arriving and Ordering
paragraphs: It is Thursday, 19:30. You arrive at the Dutch Language Café, Herengracht 13A, in The Hague. You signed up online, and your ticket was €11. A host says hello to you.
Your goal: get your sticker, then order a drink and some food.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Good evening! Are you here for the language exchange?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, I'm here for the language exchange. I signed up online.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Great. Here is your sticker. Please write your languages on it.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: OK. My native language is Japanese, and I study English.

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Perfect. Anything else?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Are the snacks included?

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: Yes, the snacks are free. Drinks are not included. You buy them at the bar.

turns.speaker: Waiter
turns.text: Hi! What would you like?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Can I have a koffie verkeerd, please?

turns.speaker: Waiter
turns.text: Sure. Anything to eat?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: What is an empanada?

turns.speaker: Waiter
turns.text: It's a small pastry, with cheese, meat or vegetables inside.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: A cheese one, please. How much is it?

turns.speaker: Waiter
turns.text: The coffee is €4.00, and the empanada is €6.50. So €10.50, please.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Here you go. Thank you!

blocks.title: Scene: Meeting Your Table
paragraphs: You sit down at a table with your coffee. A Dutch woman sits next to you. Her sticker shows Dutch, English and Spanish.
Your goal: shake hands, say your name and learn something about her.

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Hi! I'm Sanne.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hi! I'm (your name). Nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Nice to meet you too. I see Japanese on your sticker!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, I'm from Osaka. What about you?

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: I'm from The Hague.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Which languages do you speak?

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: Dutch and English. And I study Spanish.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Really? Why do you study Spanish?

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: I go to Spain every summer. I want to order food in Spanish! Why do you study English?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I study English because I want to travel and make friends.

blocks.title: Scene: The Speed Exchange
paragraphs: It is 20:00. You talk with each person for 3 minutes. You and your partner take turns choosing the language. Your first partner is Daan. His sticker shows Dutch, English and a little Japanese.
Your goal: practise English first, then help Daan with his Japanese.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Hi! I'm Daan. Nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hi! I'm (your name). Nice to meet you too.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: You can choose first. Which language?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: English, please. I'm from Japan. I study English because I want to work abroad. What about you?

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: I'm an engineer here in The Hague. I study Japanese because I'm going to Tokyo in April.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Really? How long have you studied Japanese?

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Only six months. OK, now it's my turn. Japanese, please!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Sure. Say hajimemashite. It is Japanese for nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: Daan
turns.text: Hajimemashite! Is that right?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, that's right! You learn fast.

blocks.title: Scene: The English Table
paragraphs: It is 20:30, and you sit at the English table. Sanne is there, and you meet Lucía from Spain. People can change tables at 21:10. The exchange ends at 21:30.
Your goal: ask follow-up questions, then end the conversation in a kind way.

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Hi! I'm Lucía. I'm from Valencia, in Spain.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Nice to meet you, Lucía. What is Valencia like?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: It's sunny, and the food is great. Paella comes from Valencia.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Really? Why did you move to The Hague?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: For work. I work at a hotel.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: What do you do at the hotel?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: I work at the front desk.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: How long have you lived here?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Two years. I study Dutch, but it's hard!

turns.speaker: Host
turns.text: It's 21:30, everyone. The exchange is over.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: It was nice to talk to you, Lucía. Bye, Sanne. See you next Thursday!

turns.speaker: Sanne
turns.text: See you next Thursday! Have fun with your English.

blocks.title: Speaking
paragraphs: Find a partner. One of you is the visitor. The other person plays the host, the waiter, Sanne, Daan and Lucía. Practise the evening at the Dutch Language Café again. Get your sticker, and order a koffie verkeerd and a cheese empanada for €10.50. Shake hands, and say your name, your city and why you study English. Ask at least three follow-up questions. Then change roles and use your real life.

blocks.title: Final Reflection
blocks.intro: A language exchange is a trade, and follow-up questions keep it going.

items.prompt: Would you like to go to a language exchange? Why or why not?
What three things will you say when you introduce yourself?
Someone says, I just moved here. What follow-up question can you ask?
